pr_title: ENH: Styler.to_latex(): conditional styling with native latex format
pr_body:
## Enhancing Styler to allow LaTeX Input 

- [x] closes #21673

also indirectly (by providing an alternative to DataFrame.to_latex):

- [x] closes #38328 (enh: adding highlighting options to to_latex function)
- [x] closes #28291 (enh: add option to format \hline in to_latex)
- [x] closes #26278 (easier digit format in to_latex) (although this seems to have been separately addressed)
- [x] closes #26111 (to_latex adds extra empty header row when index has a name even if index=False)
- [x] closes #20008 (to_latex shifts column names if MultiIndex contains empty label)
- [x] closes #13203 (enhancement: add optional row/col paramater to to_latex formatter) 
- [x] closes #41388 (text truncates in to_latex) 
- [x] closes #6491 (text truncates in to_latex)
- [x] closes #41636 (bug in latex formatting decimal of complex numbers)

This PR leverages the conditional rendering mechanics and unit tests in `Styler` to create a pure LaTeX version, i.e. a Styler that instead of CSS (attribute, value) tuples has LaTeX (command, options) tuples and renders directly to LaTeX with nested cell 

An extension to this is provided in another PR which converts an HTML-CSS Styler to a LaTeX Styler, and then renders in LaTeX.

### How is this achieved?

#### Internally:
 - [x] a new jinja2 template is created for generating `latex` output.
 - [x] a new `Styler._render_latex()` method is added to invoke the new template.
 - [x] a `Styler._translate_latex` method is added to make structural changes to the usual render dict `d` to make it suitable for latex template.
 - [x] parsing functions are added which do simple tasks to facilitate the jinja2 template's operation, including sparsifying multiindexes

#### For Users:
 - [x] a new `Styler.to_latex()` method is introduced to give the user control. 

## Comparison with DataFrame.to_latex()

### Input Arguments

 - Replicating the **io** arguments: ``buf``, ``encoding``, 
 - Replicating the **LaTeX** arguments: ``position``, ``caption``, ``label``, ``sparsify``, ``column_format``
 - Adding additional **LaTeX** arguments: ``position_float``, ``hrules``
 - Removing all of the **formatting** arguments: ``na_rep``, ``formatters``, ``float_format``, ``escape``, ``decimal``
     - The pattern ``styler.format(...).to_latex(...)`` fully replicates the functionality, and can be intermediately viewed in a Notebook.
     - The pattern ``styler.format(..)...format(..).to_latex(...)`` performs better formatting than a single ``to_latex(..)`` with formatting options could replicate.
     - For code maintenance it is better to only maintain the ``.format`` method rather than ``.to_latex`` as downstream.
  - Removing the pseudo-formatting arguments: ``columns``, ``index``, ``index_names``, ``header``, 
     - The pattern ``styler.hide_index().hide_columns()`` can replicate the first three, the last seemed a bit unnecessary.
  - Modifying the multiindex args:
     - Now we have <s>``sparsify {bool}``</s> ``sparse_index`` and ``sparse_columns`` and ``multicol_align {str}`` and ``multirow_align {str}``.
     - Previously the options were ``sparsify {bool}``, ``multicolumn {bool}``, ``multirow {bool}`` and ``multicolumn_format {str}``
  - Additional functionality not coded (yet?): ``bold_rows`` (maybe ``bold_labels``), and ``longtable``.

### Performance

Suppose a user will never want to create a LaTeX bigger than (200,20) so we test that size:

| Method | Time |
|---------|------|
| df.to_latex() | 151ms |
| df.style.to_latex() | 43ms |
| df.to_latex(float_format="{:.2f}".format) | 65ms |
| <s>df.style.format(":.2f".format).to_latex()</s> | <s>61ms</s> |
| df.style.format(":.2f".format).to_latex() | 45ms |

(this was improved by #41269)

Styler is broadly unaffected here by adding formatting methods, although `DataFrame.to_latex` is oddly much faster. Anyway the conclusion seems to be for this size frame and smaller performance is broadly the same, if not a bit better in Styler.

### Docs

Here are the rendered versions of the to_latex documentation

[docs_to_latex.zip](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/files/6292495/docs_to_latex.zip)
pr_comments: after this is it possible to deprecate `DataFrame.to_latex` in favor of this?

> after this is it possible to deprecate `DataFrame.to_latex` in favor of this?

yes that was the initial goal, as it is for my other `to_html` PR, but it requires your thoughts on my treatment of the **input arguments** above - whether you agree with my reasons.

> this is making Styler quite a bit clunkier. Can you propose a more modular design, e.g. we do something similar for the string formatting. Where we create a rendering engine,e g. you could have Html, Latex, Excel. Mostly could keep the code separate (the rendering vs the ops things).
> 
> Please do this as a pre-cursor. Also would not be averse to making another level here (e.g. pandas/io/formats/style/html.py, latex.py, excel.py, base.py or similar)
> 
> even though extra nesting is usually a negative, here it can provide more clarity.

I will have a think about this and submit a pre-cursor PR, just focused on existing HTML-STyler and see if it fits what you are expecting.

> this is making Styler quite a bit clunkier. Can you propose a more modular design, e.g. we do something similar for the string formatting. Where we create a rendering engine,e g. you could have Html, Latex, Excel. Mostly could keep the code separate (the rendering vs the ops things).

@jreback I am divided in my opinion. I like modularity. But: There are only two template-based methods (Latex and HTML) and one completely different (Excel). Is there much benefit in separating them? If I understand correctly, Latex and HTML share much of their functionality.

@jreback 
The progress made on this following your comments is:
    - split styler into modular components (already merged): `to_latex` is added to `style.py`, and parsing and rending is added to `styler_render.py`.
    - rename `template` as `template_html` (already merged)
    - remove all latex info from the Styler user guide. All documentation is now on `Styler.to_latex`. Zip file in OP.

Let me know how to proceed - what, if any, needs to be improved.
Will look at this in the weekend

so basically the followons are

issue_context.title: BUG: to_latex(filename) truncates
issue_context.body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
# Your code here
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Node": ["Atmosphere"],
        "Description": [
            "The Planetary Atmospheres Node (ATM) is responsible for the acquisition, preservation, and distribution of all non-imaging atmospheric data from NASA's planetary missions, including higher-order products derived from those data. In addition to providing user consultation, the node makes available a number of tools and services supporting researchers."
        ],
    }
)
df.to_latex('table.tex')
```
output created:
```bash
$ cat table.tex                                                                              (py39)
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
{} &        Node &                                                                                          Description \\
\midrule
0 &  Atmosphere &  The Planetary Atmospheres Node (ATM) is responsible for the acquisition, preservation, and distr... \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
```

#### Problem description

According to what I have read in previous issues about `to_latex()`, it should not truncate by default for the file output (and it would be a bad API if it would).

#### Expected Output

A complete table in the output tex file.

Is it possible to remove the necessity of : after bfseries
No, not unless we change how to parse CSS - a ':' is always present, and raises currently if missing.
A colon plus empty value plays more nicely with the additional wrapping options below, I think.

Right - I was thinking of parsing before we get to that step, something like:

```
props = 'cellcolor:{red}; bfseries;'
props = ';'.join([e + ':' if ':' not in e else e for e in props.split(';')])
props = props[:-1] if props[-1] == ':' else props
```
But perhaps there are various edge cases that make this hard.
@rhshadrach This looks like syntactic sugar to me. I would leave it out here and put it in a follow-up pull request once the overall mechanism is settled.
yes this change has other implications so I would also suggest making a follow on discussion.

@moi90 - I would not describe this as syntactic sugar, but rather as correcting a defect. That said, it doesn't seem significant to me, and I agree with your approach, but would like others thoughts here.

cc @jreback, @simonjayhawkins

For context: the current Styler has a method `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` which is based on the `att: val; att2: val2;` format. It currently raises an error to user if format structure is not correct. If we deviate from this for LaTeX parsing, it would probably require changing the behaviour of that method, and would represent a departure from the make _'LaTeX Styler fit the normal CSS structure'_ and, in that case, it may well be worth  asking further questions about the best way to approach this, but my preference is to keep as is.

> If we deviate from this for LaTeX parsing, it would probably require changing the behaviour of that method

I don't understand why we can't introduce a compatibility layer instead as I've suggested above. If you've said why that is not a viable route, I seem to have missed it.

because 'props' is an argument to every built-in styling method (in this case `highlight_max`), which are all ignorant of whether you are styling CSS or LaTeX. So, if you add that compatibility layer to each one of these methods, i.e. **before** 'props' are all passed to `maybe_convert_css_to_tuple` you may as well add this compatability adjustment to `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples`, which will change the operation of that method but the code will, at least, have the same effect, not be duplicated, and not pollute all the built-in methods.

For transparency, I think `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` happens late enough in the render process that a `latex` flag could differentiate between different rendering cases, and therefore introduce your code, without impacting CSS warnings.

I just preferred minimising additional complexity and relying on the user to fit the documented structure.
Ah, I didn't realize there wasn't a better place to intercept. Agreed, and thanks for the response!
Does it seem reasonable to validate position? I think the answer may be "no".
Not really, there are `h,t,b,p,!,H` but you can combine multiple and it is recommended to have a backup, e.g. 'h!'

What about:

```
valid_positions = {'h', 't', 'b', 'p', '!', 'H'}
invalid_positions = set(position).difference(valid_positions)
if len(invalid_positions) > 0:
    raise ValueError(f'Valid positions are {valid_positions}, got {invalid_positions}')
```

I too think this should *not* be validated.
LaTeX packages can define their own position specifiers and it is the responsibility of the LaTeX compiler to interpret these values.

i lean away from validation as it goes against duck typing, and it is difficult to ensure validation is consistent across pandas (or even in local functions). As moi90 mentions maybe the user has some reason for a non-standard value.

> LaTeX packages can define their own position specifiers

Thanks @moi90, this is a compelling reason to not validate.
Can just make `elif "column_format" not in table_selectors:`
I agree, but I thought this was more explicit in terms of the logic with negligible performance.

@moi90 - I would not describe this as syntactic sugar, but rather as correcting a defect. That said, it doesn't seem significant to me, and I agree with your approach, but would like others thoughts here.

cc @jreback, @simonjayhawkins

For context: the current Styler has a method `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` which is based on the `att: val; att2: val2;` format. It currently raises an error to user if format structure is not correct. If we deviate from this for LaTeX parsing, it would probably require changing the behaviour of that method, and would represent a departure from the make _'LaTeX Styler fit the normal CSS structure'_ and, in that case, it may well be worth  asking further questions about the best way to approach this, but my preference is to keep as is.

> If we deviate from this for LaTeX parsing, it would probably require changing the behaviour of that method

I don't understand why we can't introduce a compatibility layer instead as I've suggested above. If you've said why that is not a viable route, I seem to have missed it.

because 'props' is an argument to every built-in styling method (in this case `highlight_max`), which are all ignorant of whether you are styling CSS or LaTeX. So, if you add that compatibility layer to each one of these methods, i.e. **before** 'props' are all passed to `maybe_convert_css_to_tuple` you may as well add this compatability adjustment to `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples`, which will change the operation of that method but the code will, at least, have the same effect, not be duplicated, and not pollute all the built-in methods.

For transparency, I think `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` happens late enough in the render process that a `latex` flag could differentiate between different rendering cases, and therefore introduce your code, without impacting CSS warnings.

I just preferred minimising additional complexity and relying on the user to fit the documented structure.
Ah, I didn't realize there wasn't a better place to intercept. Agreed, and thanks for the response!
Does it seem reasonable to validate position? I think the answer may be "no".
Not really, there are `h,t,b,p,!,H` but you can combine multiple and it is recommended to have a backup, e.g. 'h!'

What about:

```
valid_positions = {'h', 't', 'b', 'p', '!', 'H'}
invalid_positions = set(position).difference(valid_positions)
if len(invalid_positions) > 0:
    raise ValueError(f'Valid positions are {valid_positions}, got {invalid_positions}')
```

I too think this should *not* be validated.
LaTeX packages can define their own position specifiers and it is the responsibility of the LaTeX compiler to interpret these values.

i lean away from validation as it goes against duck typing, and it is difficult to ensure validation is consistent across pandas (or even in local functions). As moi90 mentions maybe the user has some reason for a non-standard value.
